title: Ibrahim Mahama’s Vast Installations Harvest a New Future from a Colonial Past
summary: If we are lucky, we will experience several great loves in a lifetime. For Ibrahim Mahama , art has always been number one. “I always loved art,” he said. “It’s my first love. I would do anything for it.” And when he says “anything,” he means it. His work has seen him envelop entire buildings with swathes of hand-stitched sacks, and build monumental installations out of hollowed-out aircraft, colonial-era bridges, and decommissioned railway carriages. And yet, Mahama told me: “I never thought that I was going to become a contemporary artist. I only thought I was going to make art.” This changed in 2013, when Saatchi Gallery took an interest in his work, including him in the show “Pangaea: New Art from Africa to Latin America” in 2014 . “Before this, I was just experimenting in the studio, doing guerrilla exhibitions around the city and sharing my work with local communities. When the international aspect came, I realized that there was more to do.” Since then, the Ghanaian artist has exhibited all over the world and founded three art centers in his hometown of Tamale in Ghana. In 2025, he was named top of ArtReview’s Power 100. Utilizing archives, reclaimed materials, and everyday objects, his practice confronts history, global trade, and the enduring legacies of colonialism in Africa head on. His latest exhibition, “The Harvest Season,” is opening to coincide with Art Basel Paris this week at the Fondation Cartier. It’s an ambitious, collaborative undertaking which brings together nine artists and collectives, including James Barnor , Zohra Opoku , Gideon Appah , and Feda Wardak. Throughout Mahama’s practice, he transforms discarded materials into repositories of memory, recognizing how objects are marked by the economic, social, and political systems through which they have passed. “Humanity has a way of cleaning its history and its image, but material forms come to embody the histories that they live through. I like using old materials because they contain a lot of truth within them.” The exhibition features the original jute sacks that Mahama began working with in 2012, that were once used to transport cocoa beans, alongside rubber from a decommissioned rubber company, terra-cotta pots made by women in northern Ghana, and charcoal drawings on historical receipts. Together, these materials trace the entanglement of labor, commerce, and colonial history, revealing how ordinary objects can bear witness to much larger systems of exploitation and exchange. “I believe that audiences are really going to connect with this exhibition, both materially and architecturally,” Mahama said. The artist has worked closely with the architecture of Fondation Cartier’s new space, which opened in October 2025. Defined by glass and steel, with long bay windows and expansive skylights, the building offers a sense of openness that has informed the exhibition’s design. “We built the exhibition so that nothing is blocked, and at any point in time, you are able to see through it from one end to the other.” As in much of his work, scale is equally important. Several monumental installations occupy the vast spaces, commanding attention while drawing the viewer into a shared, physical experience. “It becomes so magnificent that people cannot deny it. It becomes part of their reality.” The exhibition opens with Mahama’s iconic Parliament of Ghosts (2025–26), an assembly of traditional wooden Asante stools, arranged to resemble a life-size parliamentary chamber, a space for gathering and discussion. “The stools were carved in the southern part of Ghana in the 19th and 20th centuries, and they hold a history of craftsmanship. A lot of them were broken, and we had to repair them before bringing them to Paris.” The act of repair is central to Mahama’s approach; these objects are not simply preserved as relics of the past, but also open new conversations. “Through these objects, we can ask new questions.” Historically, stools of this kind were taken from Ghana as colonial loot, subsequently entering Western museum collections and presented as ethnographic objects. Here, they reclaim a different kind of agency, inviting audiences to reconsider whose voices are historically remembered. For Season of Migration to the North (2025–26), Mahama was inspired by the Aboso Glass Factory in western Ghana. Founded in 1966, it was once the largest glass factory in sub-Saharan Africa, before being decommissioned and demolished despite community protests in 2025. Reflecting on a visit to the abandoned site, which he called a “living archive,” Mahama recalled: “There are plants, animals, and trees growing in between spaces. I thought that was important to pay attention to.” Using funds from the Fondation Cartier commission, Mahama acquired materials from the defunct factory and partly reconstructed it at the Fondation Cartier. Here, Mahama has filled a red-brick swimming pool with emerald-green bottles, produced during Ghana’s post-independence era, topped with an assortment of terra-cotta pots that evoke the region’s rich craft traditions. The artwork invites audiences to consider the fate of collective infrastructure and the possibilities of rebuilding from remnants of the past. Throughout his practice, Mahama has consistently embraced working collectively. For the artist, this approach enables collaborators to pool their intellectual resources and aspirations in order to build something that otherwise could not be achieved. Accordingly, “The Harvest Season” includes nine artists with whom Mahama has previously worked, including the radical Congolese collective CATPC (Cercle d’Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise) whom the artist visited in 2018. Its members approach art as a means of economic and political emancipation, using capital generated from art sales to buy back contaminated land to repair and restore it. Here, their surreal sculptures of animalesque figures are cast primarily from plantation-harvested cacao, critiquing the exploitative structures of the global commodity chain. For CATPC, as for Mahama, art is inseparable from the social and political realities it inhabits. “One of the most important things that an artist can exercise is a sense of responsibility. And I think it is the responsibility of the artist to find a way to redistribute art and whatever sensibilities that come along with it. Because what point is there in making art when many people cannot access it?” In this show, as in Mahama’s previous works, harvesting is not simply an act of gathering what history has left behind, but a way of reckoning with the past. “We are harvesting the decay of history, colonial memory, and our present human condition,” as Mahama put it. “At the same time, we are harvesting promises for the future. We are harvesting how we want to see the world going forward.”

title: $56.2 million Claude Monet “Iris” painting sets a French auction record at Sotheby’s.
summary: Claude Monet ’s Iris (1924–25) sold for €50 million ($56.2 million) at Sotheby’s Paris on October 22nd, the highest price for any artwork sold at auction in France, according to the house. The painting led “Le Temps Retrouvé: The Schlumberger Collection,” which made €74.4 million ($83.7 million), with every lot sold. According to Sotheby’s, this makes it the most valuable fine art sale it has held in Paris. All prices include fees. Iris carried an estimate of €22 million to €30 million ($24.6 million to $33.5 million). It topped the previous French record, €43.2 million ($48.4 million), paid for Amedeo Modigliani ’s sculpture Tête de cariatide (ca. 1909–14) at Christie’s Paris in 2010, Artnet News reported . Bidding for the Monet work lasted 45 minutes, Sotheby’s said. Jen Hua, the house’s deputy chairman for Asia, won it by phone on behalf of a private collector in Asia. According to the auction house, the work, which measures almost six feet across, is the largest painting from Monet’s 20-work “Iris” series still in private hands. “Six bidders, 45 minutes, €50 million, and a new record high for France,” said Thomas Bompard, Sotheby’s France co-director of modern and contemporary art. “Tonight, Paris belonged to Monet.” Other Monets were also sold by the auction house during the evening. Saule pleureur ( L’arbre de feu ) made €9.7 million ($10.9 million), within its €9 million to €12 million ($10.1 million to $13.5 million) estimate. Two artists also set high marks. Pierre Bonnard ’s La Cueillette des Prunes sold for €2.5 million ($2.8 million), the most paid for a Bonnard at a French auction. Gustave Moreau ’s Rêve d’Orient made €1.4 million ($1.6 million), a new high for a Moreau on paper. Sotheby’s says 74 percent of lots topped their high estimates. Three works were withdrawn from the evening sale: Paul Cézanne ’s La Ferme , Arbres au bord de la rivière , and Ciel entre les arbres , painted between 1862 and 1864, which France had named national treasures. The town of Aix-en-Provence, backed by the Ministry of Culture, plans to buy them for the Musée Granet. The three works carried a combined estimate of €1.4 million to €2 million ($1.6 million to $2.2 million). The collection sold at Sotheby’s, comes from Jeanne Schlumberger, an heir to the Schlumberger oil company. She built the collection from the 1950s with the dealer Katia Granoff. Granoff, backed by the Schlumberger fortune, bought the studio holdings Monet left for his son Miche. The sale fell during Paris Art Week , anchored by Art Basel Paris at the Grand Palais. Hauser & Wirth reported selling works by Gerhard Richter and Georg Baselitz for about $10 million each during the fair’s VIP days. The fair will now close October 23rd, two days early, citing planned protests across Paris. Sotheby’s Paris sales continue October 23rd.

title: From Carmelo Anthony to Kevin Love, 5 NBA Stars Who Collect Art
summary: Basketball, 1983 Robert Peak RoGallery Basketball at its best is a form of art. A point guard slithers and swoops through the lane. A center skies for a rebound among a sea of outstretched, sinewy arms. Even the free throw has a utilitarian, stripped-down grace. Some plays even carry the character of an abstract nightmare. The game—frantic, physical, and at times poetic—is a form of expression on a gigantic wooden canvas. It’s fitting that many NBA stars, past and present, have a deep appreciation for fine art. Several have established themselves as major collectors (some like Desmond Mason become artists of renown —and, in his case, concern ). Collecting isn’t uncommon in this world. The average NBA player’s salary for the upcoming season is $11.9 million. They travel to major cities. The offseason provides ample time to pursue interests. And increasingly, many players are finding that art is a worthwhile investment. “Rather than take that trip to Miami or buy a Range Rover or blow the money in the club, you’re better off putting it on your wall,” prominent sports agent Rich Paul told the New York Times in a 2023 feature that explored the rising prominence of NBA players in the art market. With the NBA season starting on Tuesday, October 20th, here is a starting five of all-star art collectors. Carmelo Anthony Hall of Fame forward, Denver Nuggets and New York Knicks Carmelo Anthony entered the NBA in 2003 at 19 years old, an age where mentorship is essential. He flourished on the court, winning three Olympic gold medals and retiring in 2023 as the NBA’s 10th all-time scorer. For his art education, the ex-Syracuse University superstar had Nuggets teammate Juwan Howard to explain how art went beyond “the Van Gogh s and the Rembrandt s and the Picasso s.” Anthony, who admired album covers as a child, now has a collection so extensive he cannot fit everything in his Westchester, New York, home. Among the highlights: five works by Nelson Makamo , plus pieces by Nathaniel Mary Quinn , Ernie Barnes , and Marcus Jansen . His tastes veer toward street art and photography, but one theme that particularly resonates with him is the Black experience. “A lot of the Black artists…They’re talking to me about things that I’ve gone through or been a part of,” Anthony told Cultured in 2025. “I like to be able to extend that story to people who enter the house or ask me about my collection. That experience has to surround me at home, because it’s what I relate to.” Kevin Love Power forward-center, formerly with the Minnesota Timberwolves and Cleveland Cavaliers How important is art to Love, a former rebounding champ and a starring member of the Cavs’ 2016 championship team? The five-time NBA All-Star renovated his New York City apartment around his collection . Love became interested in art in his early twenties; a conversation with Anthony, a teammate on the 2012 U.S. Olympic men’s basketball team, stuck with him. (Another art buddy: Love’s former Cavs teammate LeBron James.) Before he put money on the wall, he wanted an education. So he collaborated with British art advisor Jane Suitor, and the pair embarked on a running dialogue. “What I’m looking for in artwork is something that makes you feel something. You have a visceral response to it. In a lot of ways, it’s cathartic,” Love told Penta in September 2023, when he selected eight works for Sotheby’s “ Contemporary Curated ” auction. “I want to feel emotion. I want to feel it when I walk into a room.” Love’s collection features works by masters such as Cy Twombly , Antony Gormley , Ed Ruscha , and Gordon Parks . He’s an avid fan of Rashid Johnson ; George Condo piqued his interest in art. Both are part of a collection that is also heavy on ’80s contemporary artists such as Richard Prince and John Baldessari . For Love, these artists’ backstories also factor into the appeal. Amar’e Stoudemire Hall of Fame power forward-center, Phoenix Suns and New York Knicks Stoudemire’s passion for collecting art exploded when he joined the Knicks in 2010. He broke into the league straight out of high school in 2002, spending eight high-flying, electrifying seasons in Phoenix. “The friends that I was starting to be close with were major art collectors,” he told WhiteWall in 2016 about a group that included the artist Rob Pruitt . “And they were constantly talking about art and the art world and the importance of it and recommended certain books for me to read.” Since he retired from the NBA a decade ago, Stoudemire’s “Melech Collection” has swelled to a reported 70 pieces. ( Melech is “king” in Hebrew; Stoudemire is devoutly Jewish.) According to a New York Times profile from that time, it was “largely composed of ’80s Pop art , street art , and works by contemporary artists like Eddie Martinez and Bradley Theodore .” Stoudemire has also served as an arts advisor to former teammates and started “In the Paint,” a program where he collaborated with artists in his network “to set up art workshops for underprivileged youth in major U.S. cities,” reported Sotheby’s. The six-time NBA All-Star— who was profiled by Artsy in 2016 —has also written books and acted. More recently, he has found his way into wine and has ramped up his philanthropic efforts . Grant Hill Hall of Fame forward, Detroit Pistons The current NBC Sports and TNT Sports announcer’s interest in art was inspired by his father, Calvin, a former professional football player, who had a fondness for artwork from developing countries. As a history major at Duke University, the younger Hill discovered art could be another way to study the past. Hill’s interests are African American history and the Harlem Renaissance . Those subjects became the thrust of his collection, he told Athletes Quarterly . Hill started in 1995, early in an NBA career that spanned 18 seasons and 6 All-Star appearances, a time when art was a rare subject of locker room talk. Highlights in the 120-piece collection include multiple works from Romare Bearden and sculptor/printmaker Elizabeth Catlett . Hughie Lee-Smith , John Biggers , John Coleman , and Arthello Beck are also represented. “Something All Our Own,” an exhibition of 48 works collected by Hill and his singer-songwriter wife, Tamia, visited seven cities over three years in the 2000s. Duke University Press published a book connected to the event. “There are so many challenges facing today’s youth,” Hill told Resource Library Magazine . “I believe that an appreciation of art can help provide the forum to help tackle some of these challenges.” Darrell Walker Guard, most notably the New York Knicks and Washington Bullets; longtime coach When Walker and Bernard King, an incendiary Hall of Fame scorer, were teammates with the Knicks and Bullets, King urged the younger Walker to expand his interests. The advice didn’t click until Walker, nearing the end of a 10-year career as a defensive menace, was traded to the Detroit Pistons in 1991. “I just took it upon myself to start collecting and visiting museums and visiting galleries, artists’ studios and educating myself on the road,” Walker told Arkansas Money and Politics in 2024. “Just got hooked on it.” Walker’s collection numbers about 90 pieces. His collection, which he described to ARTnews as “eclectic,” features works by Sam Gilliam , Lynette Yiadom-Boakye , Kehinde Wiley , Carrie Mae Weems , and Hank Willis Thomas . His earliest acquisitions were pieces by Jacob Lawrence , Romare Bearden , and Robert Colescott . A hoops star at the University of Arkansas, Walker has gifted nine works—including pieces by Juan Logan , James Phillips , Herbert Gentry , and Joyce Wellman—to his alma mater. He has also donated pieces to the Studio Museum in Harlem and the Tubman Museum in Georgia. Walker has continued King’s efforts. He mentored Elliot Perry , another former NBA player, on art.

title: Art Basel Paris 2026 to close early amid protests.
summary: Art Basel Paris 2026 will close two days earlier than planned, on Friday, October 23rd, amid concerns over further protests in the French capital this weekend. The decision was communicated to exhibitors on Wednesday afternoon, according to Artnet News , which first reported the closure. In an email to galleries, Art Basel chief artistic officer Vincenzo de Bellis and Art Basel Paris fair director Karim Crippa said the event would close at 7 p.m. on Friday, citing potential demonstrations across Paris and concerns for visitor safety. Art Basel subsequently confirmed the closure on Instagram . “We deeply regret that we will not be able to welcome visitors this weekend,” Art Basel said in its statement, extending its appreciation to participating galleries, artists, partners, and visitors. The fair added that Saturday and Sunday ticket holders would be contacted directly with further information. The fair, which brings together 211 galleries from 41 countries at the Grand Palais, had been scheduled to run through Sunday, October 25th. Its early closure means that the general public will have just one day to visit, following three days of VIP previews. The announcement follows last weekend’s widespread protests across France over education and the rising cost of living, which, in places, escalated into clashes, looting, and property damage. Art Basel had already introduced additional security measures around the Grand Palais ahead of its opening this week. The decision also raises questions for the wider ecosystem of fairs, galleries, and auctions that have gathered in Paris for one of the international art market’s busiest weeks. While much of the fair’s business traditionally takes place during VIP preview days (including, this year, at least two sales of $10 million ), the shortened schedule reduces opportunities for collectors and visitors arriving later in the week to see works in person and engage with exhibitors. Other fairs are also adjusting their plans. According to Artnet News , Post-Fair, a new alternative fair in the Marais, will shorten its Saturday opening hours to 10 a.m.–1 p.m., while Design Miami Paris is monitoring developments. At the time of publication, Paris Internationale and Asia NOW had not announced changes to their schedules.

title: Our 6 Favorite Artworks Under $10,000 from the 2026 Paris Art Fairs
summary: Paris this week is a city of contrasts. Protests and unrest have given the streets a more unsettled atmosphere, even as the art world descended on the French capital for its annual flurry of fairs, gallery openings, and museum shows. With Art Basel Paris now set to close its doors on Saturday and Sunday, the week’s events have taken an unexpected turn. Still, with art popping up everywhere from the Grand Palais to tucked-away spaces in the Marais, even the most seasoned art lovers have their work cut out. Art Basel Paris 2026 is, of course, the main attraction, drawing the international art world to the Grand Palais for a suitably majestic affair. But some of the week’s most interesting discoveries were made elsewhere. Paris Internationale , in its new home beside Canal Saint-Martin, offered a characteristically adventurous lineup, while Asia NOW brought a rich mix of artists and galleries from across Asia and its diaspora to the Monnaie de Paris. Newcomer Post-Fair added a dose of Los Angeles energy to the Marais, and the intimate, four-gallery Coucou Paris is among the week’s unexpected highlights. There was plenty to tempt collectors with deep pockets, naturally, but you don’t need a six-figure budget to find something special. From delicate photography to sculptures that gave familiar objects a mischievous twist, here are six artworks under $10,000 that caught our eye. Art Basel Paris Through Oct. 23 Grand Palais. Avenue Winston Churchill, 75008 The grand dame of Paris Art Week, Art Basel Paris is back at the Grand Palais , bringing the art world’s biggest players beneath its magnificent glass roof. With blue-chip heavyweights, buzzy emerging galleries, and plenty of spectacle, it’s the week’s main event—though its run has been cut short by the announcement that it will close on Saturday and Sunday amid unrest in the French capital. Miguel Afa, Céu no quintal , 2026 Presented by A Gentil Carioca Price: $8,000 Céu no quintal, 2026 Miguel Afa A Gentil Carioca Who says you need to venture far to find a good subject for a painting? Brazilian artist Miguel Afa makes a strong case for staying close to home. His Céu no quintal (2026), which translates to “Sky in the Backyard,” captures a barely there yard scene in dusky pinks, purples, and browns, with plants, hanging fabrics, and a figure resting in the foreground. Born and raised in Rio de Janeiro, Afa got his start painting graffiti on the streets of Complexo do Alemão in 2001. He has since traded the spray can for the paintbrush, turning his attention to the homes, people, and everyday routines of his neighborhood. His layered brushwork gives even the most ordinary details plenty of character. —Arun Kakar, senior art market editor Paris Internationale Through Oct. 24 187–189 Quai de Valmy, 75010 Paris The cooler, scrappier cousin of Art Basel Paris, Paris Internationale returned for its 12th edition with a new home along Canal Saint-Martin. Bringing together 56 galleries and 5 nonprofit spaces, the independent fair traded polished booths for raw architecture, experimental presentations, and some of the week’s most exciting emerging talent. Agnès Waruguru, Heavens , 2026 Presented by Vistamare Price: €6,000 ($6,734) Heavens, 2026 Agnès Waruguru Vistamare Agnès Waruguru is happy to let her materials have a mind of their own. The Kenyan artist—who was featured in The Artsy Vanguard 2025 —often leaves drawings out in the rain and washes textiles in the ocean, allowing water to play an active role in her work. In Heavens (2026), presented by Italian gallery Vistamare , she brings this experimental approach to a modest sheet of salted watercolor paper, using acrylic ink and natural pigments to create a delicate abstract composition. Born in 1994 and based in Nairobi, Waruguru draws on techniques passed down by the women in her family, incorporating embroidery, beadwork, and natural dyes into her practice. Her works are often inspired by landscapes, though she is less concerned with recording specific places than capturing her experiences of them. In Heavens , the pigments soak, spread, and settle into the paper, leaving delicate traces of the artist’s hand and the materials’ own unpredictable behavior. —A.K. Post-Fair Through Oct. 24 74 and 79 Rue du Temple, 75003 The newish kid on the block. Formerly known as Place des Vosges, Post-Fair makes its Paris debut this year, bringing a little Los Angeles cool to the Marais. Spread across two neighboring spaces on Rue du Temple, the fair’s 34 solo and duo presentations put artists in the spotlight, offering a refreshing alternative to the city’s bigger fairs. Anouk Tschanz , Blatt , 2019 Presented by Galerie Tschudi Price: CHF 3,000 ($3,634) Some of the best portraits are of subjects that can’t pose. Swiss artist Anouk Tschanz takes her camera into the wild, photographing the plants and foliage she encounters along the way. This particular leaf, she told Artsy, was spotted on one of her walks in Glasgow. In Blatt (2019), presented by Zürich’s Galerie Tschudi , she gives her botanical discovery the full portrait treatment, isolating its delicate, perforated form against a softly blurred background. Shot in velvety black and white, the photograph draws attention to the leaf’s unusual architecture, from its gently curling edges to the lopsided pattern of holes running along its surface. There’s something rather wonderful about the fact that Tschanz found her subject entirely by chance, without having to arrange a single thing. —A.K. Asia NOW Through Oct. 24 Monnaie de Paris, 11 Quai de Conti, 75006 Paris Asia NOW returns to the historic Monnaie de Paris for its 12th edition, bringing together around 60 galleries, institutions, and foundations showcasing artists from across Asia and its diaspora. The fair offered an adventurous mix of materials, traditions, and fresh perspectives under this year’s theme of “Sentimental Value.” Berna Dolmacı, Vikaye , 2023 Presented by Vision Art Platform Price: €4,000 ($4,489) Vikaye, 2023 Berna Dolmaci Vision Art Platform Coffee, tea, henna, and waste paper are some of the unlikely ingredients that Berna Dolmacı uses in her art practice. Born in Akşehir, Turkey, in 1994, the artist began by keeping visual diaries, collecting everything from leaves and flowers to receipts and sweet wrappers. These everyday scraps eventually found their way into her collages, which she makes using discarded paper dyed with natural materials. At Vision Art Platform ’s booth at Asia NOW, I had a difficult time picking a favorite from the many works that make up Dolmacı’s Vikaye (2023), which is hung across the booth (individual pieces are available separately for €4,000 each). Built up from irregular fragments of paper, the abstract collages are dense with earthy colors, delicate textures, and torn edges. Their layered surfaces create intricate abstract compositions, with each scrap retaining something of its original character. Up close, these works look almost weathered, thanks to the natural dyes used to make them. Vikaye translates to “protection” or “preservation,” a fitting choice for an artist who gives discarded materials a second life. The only trouble is deciding which one to take home. —A.K. Coucou Paris Through October 23 19 Rue de Poitou, 75003 One of the week’s best surprises, Coucou Paris proved that good things can come in small packages. Conceived by Milan gallery Studiolo, the nomadic contemporary art platform returned to the Marais for its second Paris outing, bringing together just four galleries in an intimate pop-up exhibition. Rike Droescher, Through the Thicket , 2026 Presented by Alice Amati Price: €4,000 ($4,480) Through the Thicket, 2026 Rike Droescher Alice Amati German artist Rike Droescher has a talent for sculpting familiar objects in rather unexpected situations. In the pocket-size ceramic sculpture Through the Thicket (2026), presented by London gallery Alice Amati , the top of a gnarled, brown branch is covered with delicate white fabric. This pale ceramic hood is decorated with pink flowers and fine blue stripes, while a real clothing label hangs from the end of the branch. Here, the contrast between the rough, twisting branch and its rather prim floral dressing is particularly delightful: humorous in its contrast between its natural subject and man-made objects. Born in 1990 and based in Düsseldorf, Droescher studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, where her teachers included Andreas Gursky and Alexandra Bircken . Her practice brings together ceramics, textiles, and sculpture, often re-creating familiar objects entirely by hand rather than using found materials. She works intuitively, allowing unexpected connections between the domestic and natural worlds to emerge as she goes. —A.K. Ceramic Art Fair + Glass Through Oct. 25 Maison de l’Amérique latine, 217 boulevard Saint-Germain / 1 rue Saint-Dominique, 75007 Ceramic Art Fair + Glass returns to Paris for its second edition, bringing nearly 40 international galleries to the elegant Maison de l’Amérique latine on the Left Bank. The festive fair celebrates the expressive possibilities of these age-old media, with works ranging from minimalist to maximalist, from austere to whimsical, by artists who make these rich traditions their own. Ebony Russell, Foliate Rocaille: Blue and Pink Petite Urn , 2026 Presented by: Cynthia Corbett Gallery Price: £1,100 ($1,470) Foliate Rocaille: Blue and Pink Petite Urn, 2026 Ebony Russell Cynthia Corbett Gallery In a city famous for its exquisite pâtisserie, Australian artist Ebony Russell creates porcelain vessels that could almost pass for decadent confections. Drawing on cake decorating, her distinctive technique involves piping ruffled layers of pastel-colored porcelain by hand to create dainty yet sturdy vases. The resulting works are exuberant, recalling the decorative flair of the Rococo while feeling distinctly contemporary. Russell’s practice also engages with the gendered history of craft and the decorative arts, long excluded from art history. In her work, decoration is no afterthought; the porcelain embellishment forms the basis of the vessel’s structure. Presented by Cynthia Corbett Gallery , this small piece exemplifies that balance of delicacy and rigor, combining a whimsical appearance with remarkable control of the medium. With Russell’s work entering the Victoria and Albert Museum ’s collection in 2025, her inventive approach is gaining the institutional recognition it deserves. —Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content

title: Hokusai’s complete views of Mount Fuji go on show in the U.K. for the first time.
summary: Dulwich Picture Gallery in London has opened “Hokusai: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from the Iuchi Collection.” According to the museum, it is the first time the complete series by Katsushika Hokusai has gone on view in the U.K. The show runs through January 17, 2027. The prints come from the Iuchi Collection, on deposit at the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo. The show includes all 46 designs: the original 36, plus 10 added after the series proved a hit. Hokusai made the woodblock prints between roughly 1830 and 1833, when he was in his seventies. Each shows the mountain from a different place, season, or moment of daily life. He used Prussian blue, a pigment newly imported from Europe, to striking effect. The show includes The Great Wave ( Under the Wave off Kanagawa) (ca. 1830–32), as well as Red Fuji ( Clear Day with a Southern Breeze ) in a rare variant that, the gallery said, has never been seen in the U.K. A blue-toned print of the same design is also on view. This series of Hokusai prints has shown strong art market appeal. In March 2024, a complete set of the series sold at Christie’s in New York for $3.56 million, an auction record for the artist, as Artsy reported . The collector Jitendra V. Singh assembled the set over 11 years. The sale topped the previous high, $2.76 million, paid in 2023 for a single impression of The Great Wave . It’s a strong moment for Hokusai in the U.K. The Whitworth in Manchester is also presenting “Beneath the Great Wave: Hokusai and Hiroshige” through Nov. 15. That show pairs ukiyo-e prints by Hokusai and Utagawa Hiroshige , with The Great Wave , on loan from a private collection, at its center.

title: $10 million Richter and Baselitz works lead Art Basel Paris 2026 opening sales.
summary: Gerhard Richter ’s Rokokotisch (Rococo Table) (1965) and Georg Baselitz’ s Der Hirte (The Shepherd) (1965) both led reported sales during the Art Basel Paris sales during the avant-première and VIP days. Hauser & Wirth reported both sales, with the works selling in the region of $10 million each. Galleries reported brisk activity across the Grand Palais, with historical material by Richter, Baselitz, Lucio Fontana , and Jean Dubuffet trading alongside seven-figure sales for contemporary artists including Julie Mehretu and George Condo . Hauser & Wirth also placed works by Mark Bradford for $4 million, Condo’s Woman with Designer Shirt (2026) for $2.95 million, and a 1961 Fontana Concetto spaziale for €1.7 million (about $2 million), alongside a run of six- and seven-figure sales of works by Henry Taylor , Alexander Calder , Pat Steir , and Cristina Iglesias . “Conventional wisdom says it’s too risky to bring your ne plus ultra to an art fair, but we buck convention because the true history-making artists and collectors do, too,” Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot said on Tuesday evening. “We treat Frieze in London and Art Basel Paris as a single extended season for selling masterpieces. It’s a momentum game that extends far beyond the last day of the last fair. In the past 24 hours, we’ve sold super-rare works by Fontana, Gauguin , Modigliani , and Morandi that we first introduced at Frieze . And in Paris, we are placing equally exceptional works on our stand—true masterpieces of the second half of the 20th century by Richter, Calder, Bourgeois , Twombly , Baselitz, and Szapocznikow , along with new works by George Condo, Jenny Holzer , Henry Taylor, and Camille Henrot .” Other galleries reported comparable strength in blue-chip and historical material. White Cube sold two paintings by Mehretu, Rise of the New Suprematists (2001) and Mumbaphilia (J.E.) (2018), for $7.85 million each, while David Zwirner placed a Richter painting for $8.5 million alongside a string of six- and seven-figure sales by Robert Ryman , Joan Mitchell , and Marlene Dumas . Pace sold Dubuffet’s La chaise (1964) for just over $5 million, and Le Minotaure placed a 1922 Wassily Kandinsky watercolor for €2 million (about $2.3 million). Mennour and Thaddaeus Ropac each reported sales of historical Fontana canvases for roughly €1.75 million–€1.8 million (about $2 million), with Ropac also placing several Baselitz works ranging from €110,000 to €800,000 ($128,000 to $928,000). Art Basel noted that the figures reflect only a portion of early activity voluntarily reported by exhibitors, with the fair continuing through the week. Top sales at Art Basel Paris 2026 Hauser & Wirth sold Richter’s Rokokotisch (Rococo Table) (1965) and Baselitz’s Der Hirte (The Shepherd) (1965), both for a price in the region of $10 million, alongside a Bradford work for $4 million and Condo’s Woman with Designer Shirt (2026) for $2.95 million. White Cube sold two paintings by Mehretu for $7.85 million each, El Anatsui ’s MivEvi I (2025) for $2 million, and Tracey Emin ’s You Were Part of Me (2022) for £990,000 ($1.15 million). David Zwirner reported a painting by Richter for $8.5 million, alongside works by Ryman ($4 million), Mitchell ($3.8 million), Dumas ($3 million), and Josef Albers ($3 million). Pace sold Dubuffet’s La chaise (1964) for just over $5 million and Lee Ufan ’s From Line No. 79061 (1979) for $2 million. Thaddaeus Ropac placed Fontana’s Concetto spaziale (1953) for €1.8 million ($2.1 million) and Baselitz’s Per mano – an der Hand (2019) for €800,000 ($928,000), among several further Baselitz, Martha Jungwirth , and Bourgeois works. Mennour sold Fontana’s Concetto spaziale (1964) for €1.75 million ($2 million) and Ufan’s Response (2026) for $1.05 million. Le Minotaure sold Kandinsky’s Sans titre (1922) for €2 million ($2.3 million) and a Marie Vassilieff painting for €280,000 ($325,000). Lisson Gallery reported sales led by Anish Kapoor’ s Clear to Dark Brandy (2026) for £750,000 ($998,000) and Ufan’s With Winds (1991) for $900,000. Sprüth Magers sold two Condo paintings, The Mechanical Man and Coney Island (both 2026), for $2.2 million each. Gladstone sold Cecily Brown ’s This must be the place (2017–21) for $1.5 million and Victor Man ’s Pink Chair (2012) for $1.3 million. Xavier Hufkens reported sales led by a Charline von Heyl painting for $475,000 and a Sherrie Levine bronze for $300,000. Karma sold Reggie Burrows Hodges ’s Hutton Modesty Club: Son Runner (2025) for $650,000 and Richard Mayhew ’s Southern Border (1999) for $450,000. Kukje Gallery reported sales of two Ha Chong-Hyun paintings for up to $276,000 and a Holzer gold-leaf painting for up to $222,000. Cardi Gallery sold works by Jannis Kounellis and Bourgeois for €350,000 ($406,000) and $350,000, respectively, alongside two Agostino Bonalumi paintings for €140,000 ($162,400) each. MASSIMODECARLO reported sales of works by Sanford Biggers and Alvaro Barrington for up to $140,000 each. Templon reported several works by Gérard Garouste reaching up to €250,000 ($290,000), alongside pieces by Chiharu Shiota , Omar Ba , and Martial Raysse . Yares Art sold Robert Motherwell ’s Open #79 (1969) for $750,000. Jessica Silverman reported a nearly sold-out presentation led by Loie Hollowell ’s Yellow Brain on Soft Pink Shoulders (2026) for $450,000. Casey Kaplan sold a Jordan Casteel work for $300,000 and an Amanda Williams work for $110,000. Standard (Oslo) reported a strong presentation of paintings by Suleman Aqeel Khilji, including a work sold to a museum collection in Australia for €60,000 ($69,600) and a planned museum donation in the U.S.

title: Who Was Carlotta Corpron, the Little-Known Photographer Who Brought the Bauhaus to Texas?
summary: Carlotta Corpron lived her life in the American heartland, far from the bastions of culture in New York or Paris. But in the mid–20th century, she managed to cross paths with some of the most influential names in the avant-garde of the time, bringing the rigor and simplicity of the Bauhaus to small-town Texas. Alfred Stieglitz , whom she met in New York, offered her encouragement for her abstract prints. She worked as László Moholy-Nagy ’s assistant for a time, and Hungarian photographer György Kepes became a kind of mentor. But Carlotta Corpron never reached their international fame. Even among enthusiasts of 20th-century photography, she has remained obscure. Now, Corpron is having her moment, with a major new exhibition devoted to her life and work at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington, D.C. “Carlotta Corpron: Light Is a Plastic Medium,” on view through March 14, 2027, surveys the six bodies of work Corpron made while living and working in Texas from the late 1930s to the early 1950s. The exhibition centers on 48 prints by Corpron given to the museum by late collector Herbert Lust, as part of a broader series of photography gifts made between 2019 and 2023. Lust believed Corpron was a major talent in avant-garde photography and hoped that the museum might raise her profile. Hirshhorn curator Betsy Johnson, who organized the exhibition, said she was unfamiliar with Corpron’s work before the gift. However, she was immediately captivated by the quality of her photographs, which use light as a tool to create daring abstract forms. “We saw the work and immediately fell in love with it too,” Johnson said during a recent conversation. “It was incredibly strong, incredibly beautiful work. The vision is something you feel immediately.” Corpron’s early life Born in Blue Earth, Minnesota, in 1901, Corpron moved to India at four, where her father worked as a missionary surgeon. She later credited the loneliness of her Himalaya mountain boarding school there with strengthening her independence. In 1920, she returned to the United States, studying art education in Michigan, and earned a master’s degree at Columbia’s Teachers College in 1926. “From the early days, my mother encouraged me to think in terms of a career instead of marrying,” she later said. “I never married, and I never wanted to. I was liberated long before the women’s movement.” She would take teaching positions in Michigan, Alabama, and Ohio. In 1933, while working in Cincinnati, she bought a Rolleiflex camera. She hoped to photograph plants and flowers as inspiration for her students’ textile design, but she quickly began using it as a medium in its own right. Her first series, “Nature Studies,” which she started in 1933, evinced her interest in light, with photographs of sunlight falling through Venetian blinds across flowers or clouds pictured through shadowy angles. Corpron’s Bauhaus influences In 1935, Corpron moved to Denton, Texas, to teach at what was then Texas State College for Women. She had taken a summer photography course in Los Angeles but found it stultifying, with assignments to photograph landmarks such as bridges and courthouses. In 1940, she took the Rolleiflex to the Denton fairgrounds at night and moved the camera while the shutter was open. The swooping lines of carnival lights became her “Light Drawings.” In the summer of 1942, Moholy-Nagy was invited to teach a light workshop in Denton, and Corpron, who was inspired by his approaches, worked as his assistant, teaching students to make photograms and paper light modulators. Yet she felt that Moholy-Nagy didn’t see her as a truly experimental photographer. “He didn’t understand my need, my desperate need to work and to do something original in photography,” Corpron later recalled. Two years later, György Kepes spent a year in Denton finishing his book Language of Vision . Corpron sought him out as a mentor, and he agreed to meet with her weekly, urging her to keep pushing her work “until I photographed light instead of paper.” In 1945, Corpron traveled to New York to show Stieglitz her portfolio, who said the work opened “a new world.” Stieglitz died the next year, but Georgia O’Keeffe returned the prints to Corpron with a note that read, “He would want you to go on.” Sculpting with light In the mid-1940s through 1950, Corpron reached the height of her productivity with her “Space Compositions” series of eggs, shells, and marbles against mirrored trays and curved reflectors that distorted their forms. She preferred the morning light, working before 7 a.m., or in a small darkroom lit by a single 40-watt bulb, exposing these arrangements for a minute or two. “I didn’t plan to do anything but let the light guide me,” she said of these works. “It was more or less an exploration into the unknown.” Her “Fluid Light Designs” series took these experiments further. She bent and creased transparent plastic sheets so light scattered across them. As Johnson writes in her catalogue essay, with the camera steady she finally captured light’s movement directly on the negative. In a 1962 article, Corpron summed up her approach, writing, “Light is a plastic medium capable of creating abstract designs of extraordinary beauty and interest.” The legacy of Carlotta Corpron While Corpron offered powerful photographic force, her career was unfortunately short-lived. She met with recognition in her lifetime with a solo show at the Dallas Museum of Art in 1948. Her work also appeared in the Museum of Modern Art ’s “Abstraction in Photography” exhibition in 1951. However, even by the artist’s own account, most of her best work dates from 1945 to 1952. By 1955, she could no longer work in darkrooms due to illness. “She just doesn’t have the longevity," she said of her fall into obscurity. Her distance from the art world’s major centers quickened her fade to obscurity, though in 1975, she was included in a survey of women photographers at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, followed by a retrospective at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in 1980. Still, the exhibition argues, Corpron’s influence endured through the work of her students, including photographers Ida Lansky and Barbara Maples, whose works are described as Texas Bauhaus. “Her students were her creative community,” said Johnson. She also sees Corpron’s work as speaking to ideas that other artists picked up 20 years later. “I think a lot about her work as prefiguring later Light and Space artists like James Turrell and Robert Irwin ,” said Johnson. Johnson hopes the exhibition, which is accompanied by a catalogue, will bring new attention to Corpron’s career. “The power of following one’s vision and interests is really present in this show,” said Johnson. “In this day and age, her work offers an appreciation for curiosity, for where it can lead a person, how it can be a driving force and an organizing factor in a life.”

title: The 10 Best Booths at Art Basel Paris 2026
summary: Paris rarely does things by halves. As Art Basel Paris returned for its fifth edition, the city was still reckoning with a weekend of widespread protests over living costs and public services, some of which descended into clashes, looting, and violence. Heightened security surrounded the fair, and some collectors reportedly reconsidered their travel plans. Yet inside the soaring glass-and-steel halls of the Grand Palais, the mood was decidedly upbeat, with busy aisles, ambitious presentations, and collectors seemingly eager to do business. “This opening afternoon has been very strong, and collectors came ready to make decisions quickly,” said gallerist Thaddaeus Ropac . “Despite any worries about the demonstrations, some deciding not to travel to Paris, we already feel that it’s the most international art fair of the year.” There was plenty to support that optimism. Hauser & Wirth reported two major sales in the region of $10 million each: Gerhard Richter ’s Rokokotisch (Rococo Table) (1965) and Georg Baselitz ’s Der Hirte (The Shepherd) (1965). These heavyweight transactions provided a strong early indication of collector appetite. Under new director Karim Crippa, this year’s edition features 211 galleries from 41 countries and territories, including 32 newcomers. Its expanded footprint includes a new entrance and a larger Premise sector, dedicated to historically overlooked artistic practices, while public artworks spill out onto the streets surrounding the Grand Palais. For Crippa, the guiding principle this year is “desire.” In an interview with Artsy ahead of the fair, he described his ambition to cultivate “the desire to discover new work that you haven’t been confronted with before,” while positioning Art Basel Paris as a cultural rendezvous that extends beyond the art market. Now in its second year, Art Basel Paris’s Avant Première day—an exclusive early preview for invited collectors and VVIPs ahead of the fair’s official VIP opening—felt noticeably busier than its debut. American accents were particularly conspicuous among the international crowd filling the Grand Palais, though the atmosphere remained measured rather than frenzied. “Today was busier than last year, but the pace felt calmer,” Nicolas Nahab, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, told Artsy. “Collectors are taking time to look closely and reconnect with why they collect, which is very healthy.” Beyond the fair, Paris is buzzing with major museum exhibitions, standout gallery shows, and a constellation of satellite fairs, giving visiting collectors plenty of reasons to extend their stay. Here are Artsy’s 10 best booths from the fair. Selma Feriani Gallery Booth 1.K4 With works by M’barek Bouhchichi, Jellel Gasteli, Jessica Boubetra, Sebastián Espejo, Nadia Nejma Ayari, Monia Ben Hamouda, Baya, Sara Ouhaddou, Nidhal Chamekh, Elena Damiani, Aymen Mbarki, and Yann Lacroix. Paintings, sculptures, and photography fill Selma Feriani ’s booth, where 12 artists explore themes of cultural memory, identity, and the natural world. Among the highlights is Jessica Boubetra ’s Hybrid Orders I (2025), a towering column of glazed stoneware and lacquered steel: These twisting, biomorphic forms are otherworldly. Nearby, M’barek Bouhchichi ’s Stick charts 2 (2025), made from brass casts of eucalyptus branches and cowrie shells, references histories of migration and trade across North Africa. A quieter counterpoint comes from Jellel Gasteli ’s intimate black-and-white photographs of Mediterranean gardens, taken around 1980, which transform dense foliage into studies of light and shadow. Elsewhere, Chilean artist Sebastián Espejo presents tactile still-life paintings. Incorporating unconventional materials such as crushed seashells, marble dust, mica, and cold wax, his still lifes of bottles, glasses, and other everyday objects are richly textured and almost sculptural. Prices range from €4,000 ($4,500) to €40,000 ($44,900). Xavier Hufkens Booth 0.B25 With works by Alice Neel, Sherrie Levine, Nicolas Party, Tatiana Trouvé, Sterling Ruby, Thomas Houseago, Richard Aldrich, Charline von Heyl, Lesley Vance, Qiu Xiaofei, Louise Bourgeois, and Nathanaëlle Herbelin At Xavier Hufkens ’s booth, some of Art Basel Paris’s VIP visitors were spotted taking a well-earned rest on Tatiana Trouvé ’s enormous Sitting Sculpture (2024). Measuring more than three meters long, the painted aluminum bench resembles a series of pale, crumpled sheets draped over rough stone supports, with ragged edges and darkened crevices. It’s the centerpiece of the Brussels gallery’s refreshingly spacious booth, where each work has plenty of room to breathe. Outside the booth, Sterling Ruby ’s FLOWER (9203) (2026) offers another unusual take on a familiar form. The ceramic wall sculpture of a weathered blossom—its lumpy petals covered in cracked, mottled glazes of blue, green, and earthy brown—reflects Ruby’s longstanding fascination with material transformation and industrial forms. Among the quieter works is Nathanaëlle Herbelin ’s Boys, man (2026), a small, softly rendered painting depicting two figures grappling on a mattress, seemingly caught in a playful tussle. Elsewhere, works by Alice Neel , Nicolas Party , and Sherrie Levine round out the presentation. “There’s something about Paris: its contradictions, its restless energy, its ability to surprise you at every turn,” gallery founder Xavier Hufkens told Artsy. “ Fluctuat nec mergitur [Rocked by the waves, but never sunk], as the city’s motto goes. It feels particularly fitting this week.” The booth also saw brisk opening-day sales, led by a painting by Charline von Heyl for $475,000. Mennour Booth 0.B32 With works by Ugo Rondinone, Lee Ufan, Alicja Kwade, Tavares Strachan, Théo Mercier, Mohamed Bourouissa, Daniel Buren, Anish Kapoor, Yayoi Kusama, Germaine Richier, Manoucher Yektai, Francis Picabia, Sonia Delaunay, Alexander Calder, Lucio Fontana, Félix Vallotton, and Henri Matisse Towering above the surrounding booths at the Grand Palais, Ugo Rondinone ’s monumental stone figure the angelic (2024) makes Mennour ’s presentation hard to miss. Composed of roughly hewn, stacked stone blocks, the sculpture resembles a prehistoric sentinel, observing the throngs of VIPs beneath it. Behind the figure hangs Manoucher Yektai ’s Untitled (1962), a vigorous abstract painting whose thick, sweeping strokes of blue, green, and white offer a lively contrast to Rondinone’s imposing stone forms. “It’s always a pleasure to be back at the Grand Palais, in our city!” founder Kamel Mennour told Artsy. “This year, we divided our booth into two parts, one contemporary with artists such as Alicja Kwade , Tavares Strachan , [and] Théo Mercier , and one with master artists from the 20th century such as Francis Picabia , Alexander Calder , and Henri Matisse .” A standout of the contemporary section is Kwade’s Siège du Monde (2026), an enormous sphere of pale blue-and-white stone that rests precariously on a wooden chair, its monumental weight at odds with the delicate furniture beneath it. Nearby, Anish Kapoor ’s Random Triangle Mirror (2026)—a reflective stainless steel work—proved a magnet for visitors taking kaleidoscopic selfies, their faces and surroundings fractured into distorted reflections. There were plenty of highlights in the historical section’s impressive roster of modern masters, too. Among them is Sonia Delaunay ’s Rythme couleur (1973), a vibrant geometric painting of colorful intersecting curves that exemplifies her fascination with the interplay of shape and hue. Together, the two sections offer a compelling dialogue between modern and contemporary art—a fine example of what Art Basel does best. Prices for works at the booth start at €250,000 ($281,000) and rise to more than €2 million ($2.25 million). Michael Rosenfeld Gallery and Jeffrey Deitch B ooth 0.A48 With works by Beauford Delaney and Alteronce Gumby More than seven decades after Beauford Delaney moved from New York to Paris in 1953, a remarkable selection of his paintings has returned to the French capital. At Art Basel Paris, Michael Rosenfeld Gallery and Jeffrey Deitch have joined forces to present a survey of the American artist’s work, tracing its evolution from expressive cityscapes to luminous abstractions, alongside new works by contemporary artist Alteronce Gumby . Among the highlights of Delaney’s works is Untitled (Greene Street) (1950), a richly textured New York streetscape that captures his early modernist style. By contrast, Chartres (1954), painted shortly after his arrival in France, shows his shift to abstraction. Inspired by visits to Chartres Cathedral and its stained-glass windows, the painting marks a pivotal moment in his development. Elsewhere, Untitled (Yellow Light Swirling) (ca. 1962) exemplifies Delaney’s mature style, with radiant yellow brushstrokes dissolving recognizable forms, such as branches, into a shimmering field of color. Speaking to Artsy, Michael Rosenfeld traced Delaney’s fascination with light to his early artistic encounters with Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh . In Monet, he explained, Delaney found an “extraordinary lyrical, spiritual, uplifting quality of light,” Rosenfeld said. “When he arrives in France, he really starts to paint these abstractions, which distill nature and light.” For Delaney, Rosenfeld explained, the pursuit was as much spiritual as artistic: “He’s after an ecstatic light, a sense of God, you might even say.” The presentation brings Delaney’s paintings into dialogue with eight new works by Gumby, whose glittering compositions incorporate gemstones, mirrors, and resin. Prices for Delaney’s paintings range from approximately $400,000 to $4.5 million, with works on paper starting at $160,000. MASSIMODECARLO Booth 0.B19 With works by Carsten Höller, Matthew Wong, Yan Pei-Ming, Sanford Biggers, Elmgreen & Dragset, and France-Lise McGurn A curtain and a prominent safety warning stand before MASSIMODECARLO ’s booth , where an installation by Carsten Höller awaits visitors willing to brave its flashing lights. Inside, 7,8 Hz (Vitrine With Golden Fly Agaric Mushrooms) (2019) brings together gleaming gold-colored mushrooms arranged on a stepped red display, accompanied by a disorienting flickering light. Certainly one way to awaken a sleep-deprived VIP. Elsewhere, the booth flits between fine examples from the stalwart gallery’s roster. On the booth’s exterior, Sanford Biggers ’s Unsui (Duet) (2026) features two cloud-shaped sculptures made from shimmering sequins and felt. Hanging above visitors on the booth’s wall is Elmgreen & Dragset ’s The Critic (Trompe-l’oeil) (2026), a painted wooden vulture sculpture that looks vaguely menacing from below. On the back wall, several paintings stand out, including France-Lise McGurn ’s luminous large-scale Big Plans (2026), and Yan Pei-Ming ’s L’Exécution de l’empereur Maximilien, après Manet (2026). The latter revisits Édouard Manet ’s famous execution scene, depicting revolutionary soldiers firing their rifles at Mexico’s Emperor Maximilian, here rendered in a red-pink palette that emphasizes the scene’s violence. A quieter but equally arresting highlight is Matthew Wong ’s Shaft of Light (2016), a small, tender painting depicting a dark woodland interrupted by a diagonal beam of pale pink light. “We usually do our best for Paris, because we think that now is the most important European fair,” founder Massimo De Carlo told Artsy, noting that the gallery strives to bring a representative selection regardless of scale. “Paris deserves our best selection.” Works are priced “largely” between €50,000 ($56,200) and €250,000 ($280,800), according to the gallerist, with the Wong painting approaching $1 million. Sprüth Magers Booth 0.A22 With works by Barbara Kruger, Jenny Holzer, Walter Dahn, Sylvie Fleury, John Baldessari, Frank Stella, George Condo, Rosemarie Trockel, Kara Walker, Louise Lawler, Arthur Jafa, Ed Ruscha, Bernd and Hilla Becher, Alighiero Boetti, Donald Judd, Anne Imhof, Cyprien Gaillard, Hyun-Sook Song, Lucy Dodd, Henni Alftan, Andreas Gursky, Thomas Scheibitz, Michail Pirgelis, David Salle, Kaari Upson, and Salvo. Visitors entering the Grand Palais are immediately confronted by Barbara Kruger ’s enormous vinyl print Untitled (Forget to remember) (2024), its stark black-and-white lettering reading “forget to remember” mounted on the exterior of Sprüth Magers ’s booth . The wordplay continues just beyond it, where Sylvie Fleury ’s painting pleasures (1990) repeats its titular word across alternating black and pink stripes. Meanwhile, Fleury’s sculpture Patrick & Piet & Josef (I) (1996) presents a pair of white slingback heels accented in red, blue, and black on a low pedestal whose colored planes nod to Piet Mondrian and Josef Albers . Sharp and stylish, the works open on the booth’s themes of branding and desire. The display feels particularly timely given the strong institutional presence of two of the gallery’s leading artists across Paris. Kruger has created a monumental installation for the rotunda of the Bourse de Commerce, while Jenny Holzer is the subject of “J’ai vu,” a major exhibition opening this week at the Musée d’Orsay. At the fair, Holzer’s work IF YOU ARE CONSIDERED USELESS… (1983) is on view, an early spray-painted canvas that emerged from her collaborations with New York graffiti artists, including Lady Pink . Gallery co-founder Philomene Magers explained that Holzer’s celebrated “ Truisms ” began as printed statements pasted onto city walls, bringing her into contact with the graffiti scene. The painting belongs to a “very, very, very small group of works,” Magers told Artsy, describing it as a “really important early work” by the artist. Elsewhere, other works from the gallery’s hefty roster are present in their full glory, from George Condo ’s paintings of psychologically charged figures to John Baldessari ’s works that play with found imagery and visual juxtaposition. Prices for works in the booth range from €16,000 ($18,000) to €2.85 million ($3.2 million). kó Booth 0.P10 With works by Uche Okeke, Obiora Udechukwu, and El Anatsui Three generations of Nigerian modernism come together at kó ’s thoughtfully curated presentation in the fair’s Premise sector dedicated to historical surveys. The Lagos-based gallery brings together works by Uche Okeke , Obiora Udechukwu , and El Anatsui , tracing the development of the influential Nsukka School, which emerged at the University of Nigeria in the decades following the country’s independence in 1960. At the heart of the presentation is the concept of “Natural Synthesis,” developed by Okeke, who sought to combine European modernist techniques with indigenous Nigerian artistic traditions. Particularly influential was uli , an Igbo form of body and wall painting traditionally practiced by women, characterized by flowing, rhythmic lines and organic shapes. “He wanted to incorporate the techniques and the styles they were learning, but to tell their own stories,” gallery director Joseph Gergel told Artsy, explaining how Okeke and his peers challenged the Western-focused art education of colonial-era Nigeria. Among the highlights is Okeke’s Return of the Refugees (1967), which addresses the displacement caused by the Nigerian Civil War of the late 1960s. The conflict also shaped the work of his student Udechukwu, whose compositions employ the sinuous lines of uli to depict figures, landscapes, and scenes of collective hardship. Elsewhere, a wood sculpture by Anatsui departs from the shimmering bottle-cap tapestries for which he is best known. Created using a chainsaw to carve deep incisions into the wood, the work reflects his interest in destruction, transformation, and material experimentation. Prices for works at the booth range from €60,000 ($67,400) to €205,000 ($230,000). Mai 36 Galerie Booth 0.B51 With works by Jacopo Benassi, Irma Blank, Maia Ruth Lee, Magali Reus, Peter Hujar, John Baldessari, Matt Mullican, Rémy Zaugg, Robert Mapplethorpe, Luigi Ghirri, HR Giger, Magnus Plessen, Stephan Balkenhol, Koenraad Dedobbeleer, Roe Ethridge, Flavio Garciandía, Raphael Hefti, Poppy Jones, Kentaro Kawabata, Gowoon Lee, Thomas Ruff, Hiroki Tsukuda, Daan Van Golden, Leon Xu, and Robert Ryman. A row of five unusual photographic assemblages by Jacopo Benassi lines the exterior of Mai 36 Galerie ’s booth . Each combines a black-and-white close-up photo of a thorny branch with painted botanical imagery, mounted within a shallow wooden box and held together by metal straps. The works look precariously assembled, a combination of photography, painting, and sculpture. “He brings the medium to a completely new level, to a sculptural level,” gallery director Giorgio Dazzo told Artsy, describing Benassi as one of the Zürich-based gallery’s newest additions. “You always have this kind of fragility in his work,” he said, adding that the constructions appear as though moving one element might cause the whole thing to fall apart. The works are priced at €10,000 ($11,200) each. Inside, the presentation balances longstanding artists in the gallery’s program with newer voices. A highlight is works from Irma Blank ’s “Radical Writings” series, in which dense, repeated marks transform writing into abstraction. Nearby, Magali Reus ’s Clementine (Full House) (2024) transforms the familiar form of a glass jar into a sculpture fashioned from plaster, aluminum, and steel. Elsewhere, Luigi Ghirri ’s quiet photographs depict scenes such as a sunlit courtyard and a solitary table. Tucked away is a quieter room dedicated to what the gallery calls “artists’ artists,” bringing together influential figures including Peter Hujar , John Baldessari , Matt Mullican , and Rémy Zaugg . Lurking in a nook is a painting by H.R. Giger , whose mid-century biomechanical imagery is still strikingly contemporary today. ATHR Booth 1.H3 With works by Ayman Yusri Daydban, Abdulrahman Al Soliman, Mohammed Al Faraj, Rami Farook, and Sarah Abu Abdallah Saudi Arabian gallery ATHR brings together several generations of artists from the Gulf, mixing established figures with newer additions to its program. Here, Ayman Yusri Daydban’s mixed-media assemblages incorporate found imagery, Arabic text, and references to popular culture. One, for example, arranges decorated tissue boxes on top of each other, with vintage portraits and printed lettering. “He’s one of the artists that we started with when we opened the gallery in 2008, and he still is [with us],” gallery founder Mohammed Hafiz told Artsy. Elsewhere, Sarah Abu Abdallah ’s intimate collages draw on everyday life in Saudi Arabia. One combines a photograph of sliced watermelon with a feather emerging from a heart-shaped object, while another layers torn photographic imagery with Arabic and English text reading “But animals don’t understand poetry!” The presentation also includes works by Abdulrahman Al Soliman dating to 1991, made in response to the Gulf War, alongside pieces by a younger generation of artists including Mohammed Al Faraj . “For the first time, the gallery is working with estates and kind of modern artists,” Hafiz explained, reflecting ATHR’s expanding focus beyond contemporary art. Prices range from approximately $4,000 to $30,000. Danysz Gallery Booth 0.P12 With works by Futura Long before graffiti became a fixture of the contemporary art world, Futura was helping to redefine the form on the streets of New York. Danysz Gallery presents a rare selection of the American artist’s works spanning four decades, including several important paintings from the early 1980s that have rarely been exhibited. Unlike the lettering and figurative imagery traditionally associated with graffiti, Futura developed a distinctive abstract language of sharp lines, floating forms, and atmospheric bursts of spray paint. Pony (1982), for example, is a vibrant composition of swirling reds, pinks, and oranges, punctuated by electric-blue marks and looping white lines. “He was one of the first to go totally abstract,” gallery founder Magda Danysz told Artsy. “Some [of the works] are from the ’80s, and have not been seen for ages.” The rarity of these works has prompted excitement among longtime admirers, she added: “People who know his work are like, ‘Wow, these I’ve only seen in books.’” The presentation feels particularly fitting in Paris, a city with which Futura has a longstanding connection (the Eiffel Tower makes an appearance in one work on view). In 1981, he struck up a relationship with British punk band The Clash, subsequently joining their European tour and painting live onstage during performances. “There is a love story between Futura, Europe, and even more so Paris,” Danysz said. Major paintings from the 1980s are priced around €200,000 ($224,700).

title: Major London museums team up for South Asian arts festival in June 2027.
summary: Serendipity Arts, the Indian nonprofit behind South Asia’s largest multidisciplinary arts festival, will launch a London edition from June 19th through 27th, 2027. The festival will be organized in partnership with the Great Exhibition Road Festival, led by Imperial College London, and a roster of London institutions including the Science Museum, Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A), Natural History Museum, Royal Albert Hall, Royal Geographical Society, Royal College of Music, Royal College of Art , and the Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851. Programming will take place throughout South Kensington, including galleries, concert halls, cafés, foyers, and outdoor spaces. The festival will bring established South Asian artists and diaspora talent into dialogue with its partner institutions’ collections and expertise across art, science, music, film, and design, with London’s South Asian communities positioned at the center of the programming. An intergenerational, all-women curatorial team is leading the festival, including Veeranganakumari Solanki, Nancy Adajania, Latika Gupta, Preethi Athreya, Sneha Khanwalkar, and Elizabeth Yorke. “It’s an incredibly timely collaboration, setting the stage for the museum’s upcoming focus on the region, with V&A East Museum’s spring 2027 exhibition ‘South Asia Now: Fashion. Art. Design.’ and spring 2028 reopening of the South Asia Gallery at South Kensington,” said Kristian Volsing, senior curator at the V&A South Kensington, "I hope the festival will bring an exciting moment of cross-cultural exchange, creating a vibrant, immersive experience for our audiences at the V&A.” The London launch builds on a pilot exchange in June 2026, when Serendipity Arts presented two public projects with the Science Museum and Great Exhibition Road Festival, including नैनन की ठगी / Eyes Shall Deceive , a film, music, and sound work by Sneha Khanwalkar and artist Sudarshan Shetty , and Giants on the Move , a puppet and percussion piece staged with the Ishara Puppet Theatre Trust. London partners will also contribute to Serendipity Arts Festival’s 11th edition in Panjim, Goa, this December. Founded in 2016, the Goa festival marked its 10th anniversary last December and has drawn more than 1 million visitors while supporting more than 10,000 artists through free, citywide programming. “For over a decade, Serendipity Arts has created spaces for South Asian artists to experiment, exchange ideas, and find new ways of experiencing culture,” said Sunil Kant Munjal, founder and patron of Serendipity Arts. “Bringing that vision to London…marks a significant new chapter for us.”

title: Why Prune Nourry is Sculpting These Forgotten Women Artists
summary: In 2012, New York–based French artist Prune Nourry began spending long stretches in China. There, she started working with artisans on “Terracotta Daughters” (2012–2030), a response to gender selection in the country: 108 life-size clay sculptures modeled on eight orphan girls. The series was exhibited worldwide before being buried in 2015 at a secret Chinese location, awaiting its excavation in 2030. It’s typical of Nourry’s work, which is rooted in clay but also includes large installations and collaborative international projects. Her subject is women’s fates in an age of fast-moving science, from sex selection to genetic engineering, and the women history forgets or mistreats. To explore these ideas, she turns to multiple disciplines, enlisting ethnologists, geneticists, archaeologists, and artisans. She learned the value of building creative relationships in her own flesh 10 years ago, when breast cancer sent her from specialist to specialist in search of the “whole picture, not only of the whole body but also of the soul,” she told Artsy. Inspired by the figure 8 for its symbolism across many cultures, she often echoes that number in her series. This fall, the artist is bringing these themes together, considering a chapter of sculpture’s history that was left out with a new commission at the Petit Palais during Paris Art Week 2026. For “Visionaries,” Nourry spent time in the museum’s collections with the exhibition’s curator, Sixtine de Saint-Léger, then began 18 months’ research with four art historians. It turned out that only 4 percent of the works had been made by women, and among those, only four were sculptors. A statistic in stark contrast with the many representations of women as models, especially nudes, throughout the museum. “I asked myself if women artists really didn’t exist or if it was a matter of the way they were considered, and what would happen if we changed our perspective?” Across her career, Nourry has focused on sculpting female figures to draw attention to their plight. And she likes to think for the long term. “We live in times where everything is accelerated, with this impression of sprinting constantly. But sculpting takes time,” she said. Next year she will unveil Les Vénus dionysiennes (2024–present), a public commission at Saint-Denis Pleyel station in Paris, in collaboration with architect Kengo Kuma: 108 sculptures of women evoking Paleolithic representations. “The project started three years ago, but it’s meant for longer than that,” she said, adding that duration also applies to relationships, since she values trust and the search for meaning. Every project, she said, “has to make sense not only for me, but for the people who are experiencing it.” In 2024, Nourry co-founded the Catharsis Arts Foundation with Claude Grunitzky. Its founding project, “Statues Also Breathe,” is a series of 108 terra-cotta portraits of the girls kidnapped by Boko Haram in 2014 made in collaboration with 108 Nigerian students. Like all her projects, it relies on collaboration, combined disciplines, and duration. “Artists are to society what dreams are to the brain,” she said. “They keep society sane, translating messages through symbols, keys to the collective unconscious and the mysteries of life.” Her homage at the Petit Palais is 18 busts in plaster and marble, of women sculptors who lived in Paris between the late 19th and early 20th centuries. “It was a lot of pressure, especially in terms of interpretation,” she said. She had very few archival images to work from, mostly official portraits where expressions and poses are stern. Together with the historians, she looked at the women’s life stories and choices, thinking through three themes: motherhood, social engagement, and healing. Some are barely known. Others, like Sarah Bernhardt and Camille Claudel, are already famous. All of them aren’t talked about enough. Here are a few of them. Hélène Bertaux (1825–1909) An encounter with a sculpture by Bertaux in the collections of the Petit Palais is probably what birthed the whole project, Nourry explained. Bertaux advocated for women’s right to public education and founded the Union of Women Painters and Sculptors in 1881. “It was at once surprising and splendid, realizing that I had never heard of her and had never studied her in school, yet it was thanks to her that I was able to attend school at all.” Jane Poupelet (1874–1932) A fervent feminist and antiestablishment figure, Poupelet began her career under the male pseudonym Simon de la Vergne. She is best known for her bronze female nudes, which celebrated bodies free of the corset. She is also known for making prosthetics for disfigured World War I veterans, as noted by Nourry who mentioned that Poupelet: “created masks for Les Gueules Cassées [broken faces].” Selma Hortense Burke (1900–1995) “I made an exception to our [mostly 19th century] time bracket by adding a portrait of Selma Hortense Burke ,” said Nourry. “I love her work, and I thought it was fascinating that an African American woman was making sculptures at the time, and was recognized for it.” Burke is known for her portraits of Martin Luther King Jr. and Franklin Roosevelt. “She was also making sculptures of babies, there is this extraordinary photo of her where she’s seen in her studio making a sculpture of an infant, and the likeness is so surprising it’s hard to tell which is which,” added Nourry. Jingyuan Wang (1884 or 1893–ca. 1970) Nourry was taken with the work of Jingyuan Wang, a pioneering Chinese sculptor celebrated for her nudes of both men and women, a groundbreaking and controversial choice for a woman artist in 1920s China. “Her work is remarkable! When I look at it I see flesh. Her technique is extraordinary, and beyond technique, her sculptures exude life. It’s crazy that there is so little information about her, even though she was quite recognized at the time. She studied in Lyon then got a scholarship and went to Paris. Back in China she was a professor in Beijing,” said Nourry. Sarah Bernhardt (1844–1923) A famous actress, Sarah Bernhardt was also a painter and, as is even less well known, practiced sculpture for 20 years. She successfully exhibited accomplished marble works at the Paris Salon and even in London. Nourry and the researchers were most interested in her relationship to motherhood—one of the lenses used to study these biographies along the themes of “care/healing” and “social engagement”: “Despite having a son whom she loved deeply, she managed to have a great career, leaving him for months with family while on tours,” said Nourry, adding that it proved mothers at that time could also have careers. Camille Claudel (1864–1943) Although well known for her work today, Camille Claudel struggled to keep her career afloat while in a relationship with Auguste Rodin , whom she also worked for as a studio assistant. Despite showing great promise since her teens, letters found by Nourry’s team show that she was regularly asking her gallerists and her brother for financial help. Berthe Girardet (1861–1948) Born in Marseille, France, into the city’s grande bourgeoisie, Berthe Girardet severed ties with her family’s tradition in the trading business to become a sculptor and trained academically in Marseille and Paris. She was recognized for her portraits of common people and of her loved ones. “She lost her son at war, which deeply influenced her work: she made many sculptures on the theme of motherhood,” said Nourry. Cléopâtre Bourdelle Sévastos (1882–1972) The exhibition includes three hollow, concave portraits. These are allegorical references to groups of women from this period, like the art students, women committed to mental institutions that Nourry tried to imagine, and those Nourry calls the “legacy women,” who dedicated their lives to their husbands’ careers. For this last group, Nourry chose to represent Cléopâtre Bourdelle Sévastos, a promising sculptor who gave up her craft to run her husband’s studio instead, and did so “with a master’s hand,” said Nourry.
